facts.claim: GIA: a diamond's cut refers to how it interacts with light; brightness, fire and scintillation describe how well it is cut. Brightness is total internal and external reflection of white light; fire is dispersion of light into spectral colours; scintillation is the pattern of light and dark areas and the sparkle when moved.
GIA: shape (e.g. oval) is the outline, while cut also describes the overall design, including the arrangement and proportions of the facets; proportions affect face-up appearance.

GIA: diamond cut grades are only given to round brilliant cut diamonds because they are the only cut with standardised facets; all other shapes (marquise, emerald, pear, oval, heart, etc.) are fancy shapes.

GIA's Diamond Cut Grading System grades the cut of a standard round brilliant in the D-to-Z colour range from Excellent to Poor, assessing face-up appearance (brightness, fire, scintillation), design (weight ratio, durability) and craftsmanship (polish, symmetry).
GIA: each cut grade range covers a range of proportion sets, so there is room for personal preference within a grade; a round brilliant has 57 or 58 facets (the 58th being the culet).

GIA D-to-Z Colour Scale: D is colourless and the normal range runs to Z (light yellow, light brown or light grey); colour is graded under controlled lighting by comparison with masterstones. GIA introduced the scale in 1953 and starts at D to avoid confusion with older systems.
GIA: colour distinctions can be subtle, yet colour variations can drastically alter diamond quality (GIA also mentions price; article must not state price effects).
GIA: 'Fancy colour' refers to diamonds outside the normal colour range, generally yellow or brown with more colour than a Z masterstone, or showing a colour other than yellow, grey or brown.
GIA: internal and surface-reaching clarity characteristics are inclusions; external features are blemishes. Clarity is based on the number, size, relief, nature and location of characteristics.

GIA Clarity Scale has 11 grades, all judged at 10x magnification: Flawless (FL); Internally Flawless (IF); VVS1, VVS2; VS1, VS2; SI1, SI2; I1, I2, I3 (inclusions obvious and may affect transparency, brilliance and durability).
GIA: many inclusions and blemishes are not visible to the naked eye; most diamonds seen in jewellery stores fall between VS and SI.

'Eye-clean' is a trade term, not a GIA grade; whether inclusions are visible without magnification depends on their size and position and the stone's size and shape. No GIA page fetched today defines it.
facts.source: repo_notes: editorial reasoning from fact_09 to fact_11
facts.conflicts: Advice framing only; do not attribute 'eye-clean' to GIA.

facts.claim: GIA: carat measures weight, not size; a metric carat is 200 milligrams, divided into 100 points (a 0.25 ct stone is a 'twenty-five pointer').

GIA: 1.00, 1.50 and 2.00 carats are considered 'magic sizes' for their desirability, and a 0.99 ct diamond is difficult to tell apart visually from a 1.00 ct. (GIA also notes a price difference; article must not quote figures.)
GIA: two diamonds of the same carat weight are not necessarily equal; value and quality reflect all 4Cs, not just carat weight.
GIA: elongated shapes (marquise, oval, rectangular, pear) have a north-south axis that can lengthen the look of the finger. (Carried from engagement-ring-styles fact_17.)

Diamonds with very thin girdles or exposed points (pear, marquise) are more prone to chipping; V-shaped prongs protect pointed corners on heart, princess, pear and marquise. (Carried from active-lifestyle fact_31.)
Diamond is 10 on the Mohs scale (scratch resistance) but is not the toughest gem and can be cleaved or fractured by a hard blow. (Carried from active-lifestyle fact_29, fact_30.)
Bow-tie effect in elongated shapes and step cuts (emerald, Asscher) showing inclusions more readily are widely described in the trade but were not sourced to a GIA page today.
facts.conflicts: Needs a GIA source before stating as fact.

facts.claim: GIA Report Check lets you access GIA grading report results using the GIA report number (shown on every GIA 4Cs page); the GIA App can also look up GIA reports.

GIA: all laboratory-grown diamonds GIA evaluates are laser inscribed with 'Laboratory-Grown' and a GIA number; stones already inscribed as lab-grown/synthetic receive only the report number inscription. (From WebSearch summary of gia.edu pages, not a full page fetch.)
facts.conflicts: GIA pages variously say 'report number' and 'assessment number'; confirm current wording.

facts.claim: IGI: lab-grown diamonds IGI reports on carry an 'LG' prefix laser-inscribed on the girdle ahead of the report number, noted in the report comments; reports can be verified by entering the report number on igi.org or scanning the report's QR code. (WebSearch summary; page fetch timed out.)

IGI has publicly reported a lab-grown diamond carrying a fraudulent natural-diamond inscription, which is why checking the report online and having the stone tested matters. (Search result title only; not read.)
facts.conflicts: Read the page before citing details.

facts.claim: GIA fluorescence: reports describe fluorescence intensity under long-wave UV as None, Faint, Medium, Strong or Very Strong, with the colour noted at Medium and above; fluorescence is an identifying characteristic, not a grading factor of the 4Cs.
A grading report is not an appraisal or valuation: [[VERIFY]] source not fetched today (GIA states this on its report pages).
GIA: only about 25% to 35% of diamonds show some fluorescence under long-wave UV; more than 95% of these fluoresce blue.

GIA: fluorescence does not cause haziness by itself; it can intensify pre-existing haziness from rare light-scattering defects, which occurs in fewer than 0.2% of fluorescent diamonds submitted to GIA. In a GIA study of E, G, I and K stones, average observers detected no systematic effect, and strongly blue diamonds were seen as better colour table-up.

GIA: bluish fluorescence can make a faintly yellowish (I to M) diamond look more colourless in daylight but does not change the GIA colour grade; GIA advises viewing a fluorescent diamond in person under different lighting, including daylight, and comparing with same-grade stones.

FTC (US) Jewelry Guides: lab-made diamonds should be described with 'laboratory-grown', 'laboratory-created' or '[manufacturer]-created' (or similar) immediately before 'diamond' with equal prominence, and those terms may only be used if the product has essentially the same optical, physical and chemical properties as a mined diamond. (WebSearch summary of FTC pages.)
In 2019 FTC staff sent warning letters to firms whose ads did not adequately disclose that diamonds were not mined. (WebSearch summary.)
No ACCC guidance or enforcement specific to lab-grown diamond disclosure was found; Australian Consumer Law prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct generally. (Trade-press summary only.)
facts.conflicts: Need accc.gov.au source for the general ACL statement.

facts.claim: Kimberley Process: an international initiative and intergovernmental forum to exclude conflict diamonds from the legitimate trade; its Certification Scheme (KPCS) came into force in 2003 and covers rough diamonds.

KP definition: conflict diamonds are rough diamonds used by rebel movements or their allies to finance conflict aimed at undermining legitimate governments, as described in UN Security Council and General Assembly resolutions.
KP participants may trade rough diamonds only with other participants; every export must carry a valid KP certificate.

Global Witness (a former KP observer that left the scheme in 2011) says the narrow rebel-focused definition means the KP cannot address wider human rights risks, and that the KP has refused to broaden it. (WebSearch summary.)

Human Rights Watch (2020) says the definition ignores abuses by state actors or private security firms and that efforts to broaden it have been resisted; critics also note the scheme covers rough stones, not cut and polished ones. (WebSearch summary; HRW report not fetched.)
facts.conflicts: Fetch the HRW report directly before citing.

facts.claim: ABF (as at October 2026): travellers 18 or over can bring up to AUD900 of general goods duty free (AUD450 under 18); general goods include jewellery and watches; families on the same flight may pool allowances if they clear Customs together.

ABF: if you exceed the duty-free limit, duty and tax apply to all items of that type, not just the excess; declare the goods and provide proof of purchase; failure to declare can lead to penalties, prosecution or visa cancellation.
ABF: personal goods owned and used overseas for 12 months or more are free of duty and tax; goods on which a Tourist Refund Scheme GST refund was claimed must be declared on return.

Smartraveller: travel insurance often caps cover per item, so check limits and take extra cover for valuables if needed; valuables in checked luggage often are not covered and unattended baggage never is; keep receipts to prove ownership. (WebSearch summary of Smartraveller pages.)

GIA advises carrying jewellery in carry-on rather than checked luggage, telling your insurer your travel dates, and checking a policy covers loss and damage as well as theft. (Carried from engagement-ring-styles fact_49.)
Wedded Concierge plans venue, travel, vendors and payments anywhere in the world, with one Wedded Advisor as single point of contact.

insider_details.detail: For a round brilliant, ask for the GIA cut grade first; for an oval, pear, emerald or other fancy shape there is no GIA cut grade, so judge it face up in person and ask the jeweller for the proportions.

Before any money moves, type the report number into GIA Report Check or IGI's online verification and match it to the number inscribed on the girdle under a loupe; IGI lab-grown inscriptions start with 'LG'.

Fluorescence shows up on the report as None to Very Strong; GIA's own study found average observers saw no systematic effect, so view a fluorescent stone in daylight beside a non-fluorescent stone of the same colour grade rather than ruling it out.

A KP certificate travels with rough diamonds between countries and uses a narrow rebel-financed-conflict definition, so ask the jeweller what they know about the polished stone's origin beyond 'KP compliant'.

Proposing abroad: keep the ring in hand luggage with the receipt and grading report, tell your insurer your dates, and know that jewellery bought overseas counts toward the ABF general goods concession, so declare it on the way home.
